# 2 Maccabees Chapter 10 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic Equivalence)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 10 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_010_page_001.jpg

---

**10:1** With the Lord leading the way, Maccabeus and his men took back the temple and the city.

**10:2** They tore down the pagan altars that had been built in the public squares, and demolished the foreign shrines.

**10:3** They purified the sanctuary and built a new altar. Striking fire from flints, they offered sacrifice for the first time in two years, burned incense, lit the lamps, and set out the sacred bread.

**10:4** Then they threw themselves on the ground and begged the Lord never to let them fall into such horrors again. They asked that if they ever sinned in the future, he would discipline them himself with mercy — not hand them over again to brutal and godless foreigners.

**10:5** It happened on the very same day that the temple had been desecrated — the twenty-fifth of Chislev — that the purification was completed. The symmetry was not lost on anyone.

**10:6** They celebrated for eight days with great joy, in the spirit of the Festival of Booths — because they remembered that just a short time before, during the Festival of Booths, they had been hiding in the mountains and caves, living like hunted animals.

**10:7** They carried ivy-wreathed wands, leafy branches, and palm fronds, and they sang hymns of praise to God who had brought the cleansing of his house to completion.

**10:8** By public decree, confirmed by popular vote, they established that all Jews everywhere would observe these days every year. (This is the origin of Hanukkah.)

**10:9** That was how Antiochus Epiphanes met his end.

**10:10** Now we turn to the story of Antiochus Eupator, the son of that wicked man, and summarize the disasters that piled up during the wars of his reign.

**10:11** When Eupator came to power, he put a man named Lysias in charge of the government, appointing him supreme commander of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia.

**10:12** A man named Ptolemy, called Macron, had been acting with unusual fairness toward the Jews — making up, in some measure, for the injustices done to them — and trying to keep relations with them peaceful.

**10:13** For this he was denounced to Eupator by the court favorites, who called him a traitor everywhere he went. The charge: he had abandoned Cyprus, which Philometor had entrusted to him, and defected to the side of Antiochus Epiphanes. Finding no way out and no way to reclaim his honor, he took poison and died.

**10:14** Gorgias had been appointed military governor of the region. He kept a force of foreign soldiers and used every opportunity to press the war against the Jews.

**10:15** The Idumeans were also a constant problem. They held several key strongholds and were harassing the Jews, sheltering the refugees who had fled Jerusalem and using them to fuel their own campaigns.

**10:16** Maccabeus and his men prayed and asked God to fight alongside them, then launched their assault on the Idumean strongholds.

**10:17** They hit hard. They captured the positions, drove back everyone fighting on the walls, and killed those they found — no fewer than twenty thousand dead.

**10:18** About nine thousand more had taken refuge in two heavily fortified towers that were well stocked for a long siege.

**10:19** Maccabeus left Simon, Joseph, and Zacchaeus — with enough men to handle the siege — and moved on himself to more urgent trouble spots.

**10:20** But the men with Simon were greedy. They let themselves be bribed by people inside the towers. For seventy thousand drachmas, they let a number of the defenders escape.

**10:21** When Maccabeus heard what had happened, he called the leaders together and put the charge to them directly: these men had sold out their own people for money and let enemies go free to fight against them.

**10:22** He had the traitors executed and immediately stormed and took both towers.

**10:23** With God's help, his campaign succeeded: more than twenty thousand were destroyed in those two strongholds.

**10:24** Timothy — who had already been beaten by the Jews before — now assembled a huge army of foreign soldiers and brought in a large cavalry force from Asia. He was coming to take Judea by force.

**10:25** When word came that he was drawing near, Maccabeus and his men threw dust on their heads and wrapped themselves in sackcloth. They fell down before the altar and pleaded with God to look on them with favor, to be their enemy's enemy and their adversary's adversary — just as the Law promised.

**10:26** After praying, they armed themselves and marched out some distance from the city, halting when they came within sight of the enemy.

**10:27** At first light, both armies engaged. The Jews had more than valor on their side — they had the Lord as their refuge. The enemy had only their own fury to drive them.

**10:28** As the battle grew fierce, five magnificent horsemen appeared from heaven to the enemy's side — gleaming, with golden bridles — and they placed themselves at the head of the Jewish forces.

**10:29** They surrounded Maccabeus, covered him with their armor, and shielded him from harm, while pouring arrows and lightning bolts down on the enemy, who were thrown into total confusion — blinded, disoriented, and broken.

**10:30** Twenty thousand five hundred soldiers were killed, along with six hundred cavalry.

**10:31** Timothy himself escaped to a fortress called Gazara, a strongly fortified place commanded by Chaereas.

**10:32** Maccabeus and his men besieged it with high spirits for four days.

**10:33** The defenders inside were contemptuous, trusting in their walls. They shouted the worst kind of abuse and blasphemy down at the besiegers.

**10:34** On the morning of the fifth day, twenty young men from Maccabeus's army, burning with fury at the blasphemies, charged the wall with reckless courage and butchered everyone they ran into.

**10:35** Others came up behind them while the defenders were occupied — they set fire to the towers and burned the blasphemers alive. Others broke open the gates, admitted the rest of the army, and seized the inner courts.

**10:36** Timothy had been hiding in a pit. They found him and killed him, along with his brother Chaereas and a man named Apollophanes.

**10:37** When it was all over, they praised the Lord with songs and prayers of thanks — the God who pours out his blessings on Israel and gives them the victory.

**10:38** Not long after, Lysias — the king's guardian, kinsman, and chief minister — marched against Judea with a powerful army.
